what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Keep only the code each layer above actually needs
sections.para: Chainguard secures from the bottom up but stops at the application, leaving unused code, test-dependent assurance and a grant-more loop. The proposal is top-down: from the user story, keep only the minimum code each layer needs. Measured on sgit, 1,500 files became 428 with the use case passing, though compiled code stayed opaque.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Top-down minimisation cut sgit's tree to 428 files
sections.para: Bottom-up security leaves unused code, test-dependent assurance and the habit of granting more. Coming from the top, sgit's use case ran from 428 of 1,500 files, while other commands failed. One binary was three quarters of the bytes and only 38% of kept statements ran; removed code means nothing to patch, which can be certified.

sections.label: Bottom up, and where it stops
sections.line: Bottom-up hardening leaves three gaps and stops at applications
sections.para: Chainguard rebuilds from source and ships minimal images, but even locked-down images hold code never run, about 70% of files in the measured case. Assurance still depends on testing, and the grant-more loop remains: Custom Assembly only adds packages. Application-layer fixes such as virtual patching do not appear on its public pages.

sections.label: Top down: the minimum code below
sections.line: Ask each layer for the minimum code below it
sections.para: Start from the user story, then trace workflows, commands, modules, functions, dependency files, runtime parts and OS binaries, keeping only what the layer above needs. The higher the immutable line, the more of the system is fixed and small. Like a good linker applied to the whole stack, it kills living off the land.

sections.label: Measured on one real tool
sections.line: sgit's use case ran from 428 of 1,500 files
sections.para: sgit 0.21.0 with four dependencies ran a CI use case under coverage, then again from a tree of only the files that ran. It passed: 418 of 1,416 Python files ran and source fell from 4.72 MB to 1.98 MB. Commands outside the use case failed with ModuleNotFoundError.

sections.label: What the measurement also showed
sections.line: Compiled code, coverage gaps and coarse files limit it
sections.para: 14.78 MB of the dependencies was compiled, almost all one 14.4 MB Rust binary in cryptography, which coverage cannot see inside. Coverage missed cffi's compiled backend, which the tests caught, so passing tests are the evidence. Only 38% of statements in kept files ran, so function-level removal would cut far more.

sections.label: It did not scale before, and now it can
sections.line: Models and semantic graphs make minimisation scale at last
sections.para: Doing this by hand per application never scaled. Models are now good at understanding what each layer is for and calls, and a fractal semantic graph can hold the story down to OS files. Minimisation becomes a walk, each file's presence is explained by its path to a story, and tests prove it.

sections.label: Who does what today
sections.line: Runtime minimisers exist; starting from use cases is new
sections.para: SlimToolkit, a CNCF Sandbox project, watches a running container and claims images up to 30 times smaller, and RapidFort removes components that never run, by its own figures. Both work from what a container did. The proposal starts from what the application is for, tracing every layer to function level.

sections.label: The business model: certify what is left
sections.line: Builds traced to their use case can be certified
sections.para: If vulnerable code is never called, it should not be present; in a minimal build a vulnerability becomes a record that the code is absent. A build traced from story to OS, with graph and tests, is a high-assurance artefact a third party can certify. Chainguard is well placed to build it, or partner.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: One tool, one use case, some estimates untested
sections.para: Only sgit and four dependencies were measured once; the Python runtime and OS layers were not. The Lambda figure is from memory, Chainguard's plans are unknown beyond public pages and one conversation, and SlimToolkit and RapidFort figures were not tested. Anything the tests miss is removed, so tests define the application.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: the sgit measurement and three vendor pages
sections.para: Drafted from a voice memo of 14 October 2026 after a conversation at Chainguard's event. The measurement ran sgit 0.21.0 in a fresh virtual environment under coverage 7 against a local vault server. External sources are Chainguard's Custom Assembly overview, SlimToolkit and RapidFort, all read on 14 October 2026.
